BCB420 Assignment 1: Data set selection, clean and scoring

Differential gene expression analysis of pro-monocytes in healthy versus malignant hematopoiesis reveals systemic changes in gene expression patterns

Arhan Rupani

2026-02-19

1 Introduction

Acute Myloid Leukemia (AML) is a heterogeneous disease where different cell types contribute in disparate ways towards cancer initiation and progression. Therefore, to understand the biology of the disease, one needs to study it at the most microscopic level possible. In light of this and owing to my interest in cancer systems biology, I have chosen a case-control single cell RNAseq (scRNAseq) dataset of AML (Galen et al. 2019).

A note on the structure of this r markdown report: firstly, chunks of code which do not substantially reflect any specific learning are left out of the render however rmarkdown should be checked to understand the full extent of the work put into the assignment; then there are code chunks for which outputs are ommited but the code is shown to highlight the code itself. Finally, there are code chunks for which outputs are displayed and are meant to be read as a part of the report.

1.1 Dataset description

The dataset contains bone marrow cells, from 5 healthy donors and 16 AML patients. Hence our control condition represents healthy hematopoeisis (healthy blood formation), and our test condition is that of malignant hematopoeisis (i.e. blood formation in AML). Given the scope of this assignment, I have decided to include the following in my dataset: all healthy cells and only a single AML patient’s cells.

1.1.2 Dataset loading

For the entire assignment, I have used SeuratObject(Hao et al. 2021), a data structure designed to hold data for single cell RNAseq experiments. This is convenient because not only it efficiently stores the expression matrix and metadata, but its also highly operable for downstream data analysis as most function take it as an input. It is also an S4 object which makes it convenient to use most S4 class methods.

# Read all the files into apprpriate seurat objects and put them into their respective case and control lists

# Function to read in the count matrices
read_counts <- function(file) {
  x <- readr::read_tsv(file)
  x <- as.data.frame(x)
  genes <- x$Gene
  x <- x[, -1]
  rownames(x) <- genes
  return(as.matrix(x))
}

# Function to read in metadata
read_meta <- function(file) {
  y <- readr::read_tsv(file)
  y <- as.data.frame(y)
  cells <- y$Cell
  y <- y[, -1]
  rownames(y) <- cells
  return(y)
}

#1. Healthy data preparation

## I am hard coding the paths but ideally you want to use getwd()
counts_files <- list.files("/home/rstudio/projects/data/healthy", pattern = "*.dem.txt", full.names = TRUE)
meta_files <- list.files("/home/rstudio/projects/data/healthy", pattern = "*.anno.txt", full.names = TRUE)
healthy_samp_names <- str_extract(counts_files, "BM[^.]+")

counts <- purrr::map(counts_files, read_counts)
meta <- purrr::map(meta_files, read_meta)

## Create seurat object
healthy_objs <- purrr::map2(counts, meta, ~ SeuratObject::CreateSeuratObject(counts = as(.x, "sparseMatrix"), meta.data = .y))
names(healthy_objs) <- healthy_samp_names

1.3 Experiment Hypotheis

Following exploratory analysis of the dataset, I found that that the most abundant cell type in the AML pateint sample was Pro-Monocytes. Therefore we are interested in studying gene expression changes in particularly pro-monocytes in healthy hematopoeisis vs malignant hematopoesis.

This is also interesting because we are studying AML, which is a malignancy of myeloid cells, and pro-monocytes are a part of the myeloid lineage

NOTE: Coding help from Gen.AI was seeked to figure out to how fetch data from different mirrors while being able to catch any errors in connecting to the mart itslef and during the retrival of information.

# Check mapping of all genes to HUGO symbols
# Get all gene names from the dataset
all_genes <- Features(case_cont_data)

## Total genes in dataset: 27899
# Connect to biomaRt with error handling
library(biomaRt)

# Increase timeout
options(timeout = 300)

# Try to connect to biomaRt with fallback mirrors
mart <- NULL
mirrors <- c(
  "https://asia.ensembl.org",
  "https://useast.ensembl.org",
  "https://www.ensembl.org"
)

for (mirror in mirrors) {
  cat("Attempting to connect to:", mirror, "\n")
  tryCatch({
    mart <- useMart("ensembl", 
                    dataset = "hsapiens_gene_ensembl",
                    host = mirror)
    cat("Successfully connected to:", mirror, "\n\n")
    break
  }, error = function(e) {
    cat("Failed to connect to", mirror, ":", e$message, "\n")
  })
}
## Attempting to connect to: https://asia.ensembl.org 
## Failed to connect to https://asia.ensembl.org : HTTP 403 Forbidden. 
## Attempting to connect to: https://useast.ensembl.org 
## Successfully connected to: https://useast.ensembl.org
if (is.null(mart)) {
  stop("Failed to connect to any Ensembl mirror. Please check your internet connection and try again later.")
}

# Query all genes with error handling and retry logic
chunk_size <- 5000
n_chunks <- ceiling(length(all_genes) / chunk_size)
all_results <- list()
failed_chunks <- c()

for (i in 1:n_chunks) {
  start_idx <- (i - 1) * chunk_size + 1
  end_idx <- min(i * chunk_size, length(all_genes))
  
  cat("Processing chunk", i, "of", n_chunks, 
      "(genes", start_idx, "to", end_idx, ")...\n")
  
  chunk_genes <- all_genes[start_idx:end_idx]
  
  # Retry logic
  max_attempts <- 3
  attempt <- 1
  success <- FALSE
  chunk_results <- NULL
  
  while (attempt <= max_attempts && !success) {
    tryCatch({
      chunk_results <- getBM(
        attributes = c('hgnc_symbol', 'external_gene_name', 'gene_biotype'),
        filters = 'hgnc_symbol',
        values = chunk_genes,
        mart = mart
      )
      all_results[[i]] <- chunk_results
      success <- TRUE
      cat("  ✓ Chunk", i, "completed successfully\n")
    }, error = function(e) {
      cat("  ✗ Attempt", attempt, "failed:", conditionMessage(e), "\n")
      if (attempt < max_attempts) {
        wait_time <- attempt * 5  # Increasing wait time
        cat("  Waiting", wait_time, "seconds before retry...\n")
        Sys.sleep(wait_time)
      }
      attempt <<- attempt + 1
    })
  }
  
  if (!success) {
    cat("  ⚠ WARNING: Chunk", i, "failed after", max_attempts, "attempts\n")
    failed_chunks <- c(failed_chunks, i)
    all_results[[i]] <- data.frame()  # Empty data frame as placeholder
  }
  
  # Delay between successful chunks to avoid overwhelming server
  if (success && i < n_chunks) {
    Sys.sleep(2)
  }
}

2.2 Normalization

2.2.1 Rationale for normalization method

For single-cell RNA-seq data, I chose to use **log-normalization*, which is routinely used in scRNAseq, from Seurat’s NormalizeData() function (Hao et al. 2021) . This method performs the following steps:

  1. Normalizes gene expression measurements for each cell by the total expression
  2. Multiplies by a scale factor (10,000 by default)
  3. Log-transforms the result (natural log)
case_cont_data <- NormalizeData(case_cont_data)

To assess the effectiveness of normalization, I compared the distribution of total counts per cell before and after normalization.

# Join layers first
case_cont_data <- JoinLayers(case_cont_data)

# Extract sum of counts for each cell
counts_before <- colSums(LayerData(case_cont_data, assay = "RNA", layer = "counts"))
counts_after <- colSums(LayerData(case_cont_data, assay = "RNA", layer = "data"))

# Create comparison dataframe
comparison_df <- data.frame(
  Before_Normalization = counts_before,
  After_Normalization = counts_after
)

# Reshape to long format
comparison_long <- pivot_longer(comparison_df, 
                                 cols = c("Before_Normalization", "After_Normalization"),
                                 names_to = "Stage", 
                                 values_to = "Sum_Counts")

# Create histogram
ggplot(comparison_long, aes(x = Sum_Counts, fill = Stage)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100) +
  facet_wrap(~Stage, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Sum of Counts per Cell: Before vs After Normalization",
    x = "Sum of Counts",
    y = "Number of Cells"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Figure 2: Distribution of sum of counts per cell before and after LogNormalize normalization. The left panel shows raw counts with high variability across cells, while the right panel shows normalized data with reduced technical variation.

Interpretation: The before normalization histogram shows the raw count distribution with high cell-to-cell variability in total counts, reflecting technical variation in sequencing depth. After LogNormalize, the data is log-transformed and scaled, which compresses the range and centers the distribution. This normalization step is crucial for making cells comparable accounting for variable sequencing depths for each cell.

Note on final dataset format: While the assignment specifies producing a dataframe with HUGO symbols as rownames and samples as columns, single-cell data is inherently different from bulk RNA-seq. In scRNA-seq, each “sample” is a single cell (12,680 cells in our case), making a traditional gene × sample matrix impractical. Instead, I have retained the data in a Seurat object format, which efficiently stores: - Gene expression matrix (genes × cells) - Cell metadata (condition, cell type, etc.) - Normalized data in separate layers

2.3 Differential Gene Expression

2.3.1 Model design

For differential expression analysis, I used Seurat’s FindMarkers() function (Hao et al. 2021), which implements: - Wilcoxon rank sum test (default): A non-parametric test suitable for scRNA-seq data - Model design: Comparing two conditions within a single cell type - Condition 1 (ident.1): ProMono_healthy (control) - Condition 2 (ident.2): ProMono-like_cancer (case)

First I run the basic pipeline to fully process the single-cell data, this includes finding top variable genes, performing principle component analysis, unsepervised clustering (not needed here though), and umap visualization. Finally then, I ask what genes are differentially upregulates/downregulated in different conditions for cells of the same type.

# Identify differential expressed genes across conditions

#3. Run Pipeline
case_cont_data <- FindVariableFeatures(case_cont_data)
## Finding variable features for layer counts
case_cont_data <- ScaleData(case_cont_data)
## Centering and scaling data matrix
case_cont_data <- RunPCA(case_cont_data)
## PC_ 1 
## Positive:  MALAT1, TMSB4X, JUN, SYNE2, CCL5, RNA28S, ETS1, NFKBIA, IFITM1, CTSS 
##     IL32, CD3D, BIRC3, SYNE1, NEAT1, IL7R, GNLY, TXNIP, CD3G, CD2 
##     SLFN5, CD8A, PRDM1, KLRK1, SRGN, GZMA, CD69, BCL11B, SLAMF7, IKZF3 
## Negative:  CA1, AHSP, RHAG, HBD, HBB, TUBB, PCLAF, TOP2A, CENPF, MKI67 
##     ANK1, CENPU, SPTA1, TUBA1B, PRDX2, NUSAP1, HIST1H4C, STMN1, HIST1H1B, DHFR

top_down$Direction <- "Downregulated"
top_down <- top_down[, c("Gene", "avg_log2FC", "p_val_adj", "Direction")]

top_genes_table$avg_log2FC <- round(top_genes_table$avg_log2FC, 3)

2.3.2 Volcano plot visualization

# Visualisation
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

# Add a column for significance
promono.case_cond.response$gene <- rownames(promono.case_cond.response)
promono.case_cond.response$diffexpressed <- "NO"
promono.case_cond.response$diffexpressed[promono.case_cond.response$avg_log2FC > 0.6 & promono.case_cond.response$p_val_adj < 0.05] <- "UP"
promono.case_cond.response$diffexpressed[promono.case_cond.response$avg_log2FC < -0.6 & promono.case_cond.response$p_val_adj < 0.05] <- "DOWN"

# Label top genes
promono.case_cond.response$delabel <- NA
promono.case_cond.response$delabel[promono.case_cond.response$diffexpressed != "NO"] <- promono.case_cond.response$gene[promono.case_cond.response$diffexpressed != "NO"]

# Plot
ggplot(promono.case_cond.response, aes(x = avg_log2FC, y = -log10(p_val_adj), col = diffexpressed, label = delabel)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.6, 0.6), col = "gray", linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), col = "gray", linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_point(size = 2) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "gray", "red"),
                     labels = c("Downregulated", "Not significant", "Upregulated")) +
  geom_text_repel(max.overlaps = 10, size = 3) +
  labs(x = "log2 Fold Change", y = "-log10 Adjusted P-value", 
       title = "ProMono: Healthy vs Cancer") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank())

Volcano plot showing differential gene expression between healthy and cancer pro-monocytes. Each point represents a gene. The x-axis shows log2 fold change (positive values indicate higher expression in healthy cells, negative values indicate higher expression in cancer cells). The y-axis shows statistical significance as -log10(adjusted p-value). Red points indicate significantly upregulated genes in healthy cells (log2FC > 0.6, adj. p-value < 0.05), blue points indicate significantly upregulated genes in cancer cells (log2FC < -0.6, adj. p-value < 0.05), and gray points are not significantly different. Vertical dashed lines mark the fold change threshold (±0.6), and the horizontal dashed line marks the significance threshold (adj. p-value = 0.05). Gene labels are shown for the most significant differentially expressed genes [Wickham (2016)](Slowikowski 2023).

Interpretation: The volcano plot reveals clear transcriptional differences between healthy and cancer pro-monocytes. Genes on the right (positive log2FC) are upregulated in healthy cells relative to cancer, while genes on the left are downregulated. The vertical spread (-log10 p-value) indicates statistical confidence, with genes at the top showing the strongest evidence for differential expression.

2.3.3 Statistical thresholds and results

Thresholds used: - P-value threshold: p_val_adj < 0.05 (adjusted p-value using Bonferroni correction) - Log2 fold change threshold: |log2FC| > 0.6 (approximately 1.5-fold change)

Rationale for thresholds: - Adjusted p-value < 0.05: Standard statistical significance threshold after multiple hypothesis correction - Log2FC > 0.6: Biological significance threshold captures genes with meaningful expression changes while filtering out minor fluctuations

# Calculate number of significant genes
sig_genes <- promono.case_cond.response[promono.case_cond.response$p_val_adj < 0.05, ]
up_genes <- sig_genes[sig_genes$avg_log2FC > 0.6, ]
down_genes <- sig_genes[sig_genes$avg_log2FC < -0.6, ]

cat("=== DIFFERENTIAL EXPRESSION SUMMARY ===\n")
## === DIFFERENTIAL EXPRESSION SUMMARY ===
cat("Total genes tested:", nrow(promono.case_cond.response), "\n")
## Total genes tested: 10443
cat("Significantly DE genes (p_val_adj < 0.05):", nrow(sig_genes), "\n")
## Significantly DE genes (p_val_adj < 0.05): 1444
cat("Upregulated genes (log2FC > 0.6):", nrow(up_genes), "\n")
## Upregulated genes (log2FC > 0.6): 817
cat("Downregulated genes (log2FC < -0.6):", nrow(down_genes), "\n")
## Downregulated genes (log2FC < -0.6): 387

2.3.4 Multiple hypothesis testing correction

Method used: Bonferroni correction (default in Seurat’s FindMarkers)

Why Bonferroni? Standard in scRNA-seq and Widely accepted in the field. Alternatively we could have also used Benjamini-Hochberg.

2.3.5 Heatmap of top differentially expressed genes

library(pheatmap)
library(pheatmap)

# Get top 50 DE genes (25 up, 25 down)
top_genes <- promono.case_cond.response %>%
  filter(diffexpressed != "NO") %>%
  arrange(p_val_adj) %>%
  head(50) %>%
  rownames()

# Subset Seurat object to pro-monocytes only
promono_cells <- case_cont_data[, case_cont_data$`CellType-condition` %in% 
                                   c("ProMono-healthy", "ProMono-like-cancer")]

# Scale the data for these specific genes if not already done
promono_cells <- ScaleData(promono_cells, features = top_genes)

# Extract scaled data for heatmap
heatmap_data <- LayerData(promono_cells, assay = "RNA", layer = "scale.data")[top_genes, ]

# Create annotation for columns (cells)
cell_annotation <- data.frame(
  Condition = promono_cells$condition,
  row.names = colnames(heatmap_data)
)

# Plot heatmap
pheatmap(heatmap_data,
         annotation_col = cell_annotation,
         show_colnames = FALSE,
         show_rownames = TRUE,
         cluster_rows = TRUE,
         cluster_cols = TRUE,
         scale = "none",  # Already scaled
         color = colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(100),
         main = "Top 50 DE Genes: Healthy vs Cancer Pro-Monocytes")

Heatmap of the top 50 differentially expressed genes between healthy and cancer pro-monocytes. Rows represent genes and columns represent individual cells. Gene expression values are scaled. Cells are annotated by condition (healthy vs cancer) and hierarchically clustered based on expression patterns. Color intensity indicates relative expression level: red (high), white (medium), blue (low) (Kolde 2019).

Do conditions cluster together?

Yes, the heatmap demonstrates clear clustering of cells by condition (healthy vs cancer). This is evident from:

  1. Column clustering: Cells from the same condition group together, indicating that cancer and healthy pro-monocytes have distinct gene expression profiles
  2. Gene clustering: Genes cluster into groups that are specifically upregulated or downregulated in one condition

The clear separation validates our differential expression analysis.

3 Discussion and Conclusion

To summarise, I indeed find patterns of biological organisation, indicated by clear seperation of two conditions, in the heatmap visualisation upon differential gene expression analysis. Remarkably, this suggests that malignant transformation leads to substantial transcriptional reprogramming in pro-monocytes. It would be interesting to further this analysis vy inclusing other patients and looking for ubiquitously dysregulated genes and pathways.

Finally, as the part of this assignment, the following questions needed to be answered. Some have an anchor to the section where they are answered and some are answered below:

  • Why is the dataset of interest to you?

  • What are the control and test conditions of the dataset?

  • How many samples in each of the conditions of your dataset?

  • Were there expression values that were not unique for specific genes? How did you handle these?

  • Were there expression values that could not be mapped to current HUGO symbols?

  • Were there any outliers in your dataset? How were they handled in the originating paper? How many outliers were removed?

    No outliers were present as the original paper had already performed quality control and uploaded this dataset on GEO (Galen et al. 2019). The original study had removed cells with very low total gene counts and genes which were detected in extremely few cells. Hence, I did not remove any cells or genes (outliers).

  • How did you handle replicates?

    Sample structure:

    • 5 healthy donors (biological replicates for control condition)
    • 1 AML patient (for test condition)

    Analysis approach: Single-cell analysis treats individual cells as technical replicates within biological conditions. Each cell is an independent measurement.

    Statistical power: Thousands of cells per condition provide robust statistical power despite having only one AML patient.

  • What is the final coverage of your dataset?
